analysis.one_liner: Imposes accountability rules on for-profit colleges and strengthens loan discharge rights for defrauded students.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2025 and referred to two House committees, where it has received no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes strict federal rules into law for colleges that live off federal student aid, with the sharpest measures aimed at for-profit schools. It would cut off federal aid to career-training programs whose graduates can't earn enough to repay their loans, restore students' right to sue schools in court instead of being forced into arbitration, bar schools from withholding transcripts over unpaid balances, and create an enforcement unit and a multi-agency task force to police for-profit education. It would also make it easier for students misled by a school to have their federal loans discharged.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and former students at colleges with poor outcomes, especially for-profit schools, and student loan borrowers who were misled by aggressive recruiting or false job and earnings claims. Taxpayers also benefit from reduced losses when bad schools collapse and loans are forgiven.

how_it_helps.text: Programs whose graduates consistently carry debt-to-earnings rates the bill defines as too high, or earn no more than a high school graduate, would lose access to federal student aid and could not offer a similar program for three years [S3].

Colleges could not force students into mandatory arbitration or bar them from going to court, could not enforce class-action waivers, and could not withhold official transcripts because a student owes money; students also get a private right of action to sue over substantial misrepresentations [S3].

The bill writes strong borrower-defense and closed-school discharge rules into statute, including automatic discharge for students at schools that closed and group discharges without individual applications [S3].

It creates an enforcement unit inside the Office of Federal Student Aid with subpoena power, a For-Profit Education Oversight Coordination Committee spanning nine federal agencies, and a public complaint tracking system; civil penalties for misrepresentations rise from $25,000 to $100,000 per violation [S3].
Institutions would have to spend at least 30% of tuition and fee revenue on actual instruction, with marketing, recruiting, and executive pay counted against them in reporting [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit colleges and career-training schools whose programs fail the debt-to-earnings or earnings-premium tests would lose federal student aid revenue. Loan servicers, third-party servicers, and accreditors face expanded oversight and penalty exposure. Nonprofit colleges also face the 30% instructional-spending floor and the arbitration and transcript rules, though the sharpest tools target the for-profit sector.

drawbacks.text: The bill would shift the administration of the aid rules back toward a heavier, more intrusive regulatory model — opponents have long argued such rules push schools out of serving low-income and adult students, and the bill exempts its rules from normal negotiated rulemaking procedures (sections 492), concentrating power with the Department of Education [S3].

Some costs are passed to all colleges: the mandatory 30% instruction-spending floor and new reporting on marketing and recruiting spending apply to every Title IV institution, not just bad actors, which could burden small nonprofit schools [S3].
Automatic and group discharges of loans could increase costs to taxpayers, which the Treasury absorbs when loans are forgiven [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For students and borrowers the protections are concrete: relief for people defrauded by a school, court access, transcripts that can't be held hostage, and warnings about programs with poor outcomes. The main counterweight is the cost to colleges of compliance and to taxpayers of loan discharges, plus the risk that stricter rules could shrink the supply of career-training programs. The design deliberately targets the worst outcomes with financial tests rather than banning any sector outright.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Education and Workforce and Judiciary committees, and neither has taken it up; it sits there with no scheduled action.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Takano introduced the bill on April 10, 2025, joined by five Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce and the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action appears in the bill's action history as of now, and the Congress runs through January 2027 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For-profit colleges and their investors, which keep receiving federal student aid without the debt-to-earnings cutoffs, spending floors, or enforcement unit the bill would have imposed. Students and borrowers remain under whatever protections the Department chooses to keep in place by regulation, which can change with each administration.

against.name: For-profit college industry
against.what_they_did: The for-profit college sector has a long public record of lobbying and litigating against gainful-employment rules, borrower-defense regulations, and enforcement measures like those in this bill

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; the House majority is Republican and no Republican has cosponsored or scheduled action on the bill.

industries.note: Programs whose graduates can't repay their debt or out-earn high school graduates would lose federal aid, the schools face tougher certification, higher civil penalties, and a new interagency enforcement committee. The whole bill is aimed primarily at this sector, and the schools' interest in keeping federal aid flowing runs against the students who borrow to attend them.

industries.industry: Student loan servicers and third-party servicers
industries.note: These contractors would face complaint tracking, expanded oversight, penalty liability, and exposure to false-claims liability for institutional misconduct they touch, reducing the flexibility under which servicers profit.
Accreditors would have to assess risk at institutions and programs and justify their monitoring, an added burden on bodies whose revenues come from the institutions they accredit.

They face the 30% instruction-spending floor, the arbitration and transcript bans, and new spending disclosures, but the bill's financial-value cutoffs and for-profit oversight committee leave their core aid eligibility intact.

Colleges could no longer route student disputes into mandatory arbitration or hold transcripts over unpaid balances, closing off practices that are lucrative for schools and debt collectors at students' expense.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican House majority, referral to two committees, no hearing, and only Democratic cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to advance this Congress; at best its ideas could resurface if control of government changes, but it will likely die in committee in January 2027.
